content: Key populations are at a higher risk of HIV infection primarily because the prevalence of HIV within their sexual or needle-sharing networks is already elevated. While individuals in the general population may also engage in high-risk behaviors, such as frequent vaginal or anal sex without condoms, their likelihood of encountering an HIV-positive partner is significantly lower compared to members of key populations. The ethical considerations surrounding HIV surveys, particularly the return of test results to participants, have evolved over time. National governments, donors, and United Nations (UN) agencies increasingly demand data on access to HIV services, given the critical role of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in both treatment and prevention. Engaging target populations and other stakeholders has become essential for survey planning and implementation. Additionally, providing third-party researchers with broader access to survey data is now a priority. The objectives of these guidelines include updating the overall approach and methodology of BBS in light of advancements over the past decade, improving the quality of BBS through comprehensive guidance on sampling methods and data collection, ensuring the collection of representative and actionable data for public health programming, and promoting the use of survey findings to enhance service delivery, monitoring, evaluation, and policy development. These guidelines are intended for policymakers, organizations, and technical staff involved in planning or conducting BBS among key and at-risk populations. While applicable in all settings, they are particularly relevant for lowand middle-income countries. Policies that criminalize the behaviors of key populations or restrict their access to services can further increase their risk of acquiring and transmitting HIV. For instance, over two-thirds of sub-Saharan African countries criminalize same-sex practices, and criminalized populations often receive less than 25% of intended human-rights-focused interventions. This lack of access to necessary services leaves them vulnerable. In countries where the behaviors of sex workers (SW), men who have sex with men (MSM), transgender individuals (TG), or people who inject drugs (PWID) are criminalized and such laws are enforced, access to services is even more severely impacted. Conversely, anti-discrimination laws are associated with improved access to prevention services for these populations. Socio-structural factors such as stigma, harassment, marginalization, and lack of social support contribute to higher rates of HIV transmission and other infections, particularly among sex workers, sexual minorities, and people who inject drugs. Social rejection or marginalization can lead to isolation, unemployment, poverty, unstable living conditions, or homelessness. Fear of police harassment, arrest, or discrimination by healthcare providers further discourages key populations from seeking prevention and treatment services. For example, a global assessment of HIV prevention services for MSM in 147 lowand middle-income countries found that 55% of these countries could not document the provision of even basic HIV-related services. Additionally, only 4% of PWID with HIV who are eligible for treatment worldwide are receiving ART. The rationale for these updated guidelines stems from the significant changes in the HIV landscape since the introduction of combination antiretroviral therapy in the 2000s, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Data needs and survey methods have also evolved, with new sampling techniques such as respondent-driven sampling (RDS) emerging. While BBS remains a critical data source for understanding HIV epidemics among key populations, it is complemented by other data sources, including population size estimation, mapping, HIV case surveillance, cohort studies, program-based data, and upstream data on policy, stigma, and discrimination. These guidelines are not intended for general population or household-based surveys, as other resources are available for those purposes. Instead, they provide a comprehensive resource for conducting BBS, focusing on practical aspects such as formative assessment, survey design, protocol development, data collection, analysis, and dissemination of findings. The guidelines are divided into three main sections: survey preparation, survey implementation and quality assurance, and data analysis and use. Supplementary materials include appendices, questionnaire modules, indicators, and a glossary. The collection of standardized data is central to any survey activity. The data instruments included in these guidelines have been updated to include questions on the continuum of care and are organized into modules focused on specific topics. This modular approach allows users to tailor data collection to local priorities and the needs of each target population. Core variables are also available in ready-to-use electronic formats. Standardized indicators facilitate comparisons of the HIV epidemic across different time points, locations, or populations. The supplementary materials include resources such as references for further reading, examples of protocol checklists, survey consent language, and data analysis commands for commonly used software packages. These updated guidelines aim to enable the collection of more detailed, accurate, and relevant data among populations at risk for HIV, ultimately supporting more effective HIV services, advocacy, and policymaking.
